flora-balga.name: Balga
flora-balga.fact: Grows only a centimetre or so a year, so a tall one can be centuries old. Its blackened trunk shrugs off bushfire, and a fire makes it flower all the more.
flora-balga.noongar: people named it balga. Its gum, spears for fishing and fire drills all came from it, and the bardi grubs living inside were good tucker.

flora-parrot-bush.name: Parrot bush
flora-parrot-bush.fact: It pours out nectar for honeyeaters, and black cockatoos and ringneck parrots feast on its seed. Fire kills it, but it drops so much seed that it bounces straight back.
flora-parrot-bush.noongar: names for it include budjan and butyak.

flora-coast-sword-sedge.name: Sword-sedge
flora-coast-sword-sedge.fact: Big clumps of flat, sharp-pointed leaves, as long as swords, with spiky brown flower heads standing on tall stalks through summer and autumn.
flora-coast-sword-sedge.noongar: people call it kerbein, and ate the tender part of its stem all year round.

flora-prickly-conostylis.name: Conostylis
flora-prickly-conostylis.fact: Aculeata means “with prickles”: its strappy leaves are edged with spines. In spring, bright yellow, furry tube flowers cluster on tall stalks.

flora-coast-daisy-bush.name: Daisy-bush
flora-coast-daisy-bush.fact: A silvery, scented shrub that thrives in the salt wind. The Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh is said to have cooked with its leaves on Rottnest in 1696.

flora-peppermint.name: Peppermint
flora-peppermint.fact: The critically endangered western ringtail possum depends on it, feeding at night on its young leaves, flowers and fruit.
flora-peppermint.noongar: people call it wonnil (spellings vary). Its leaves were used as an antiseptic, and young trunks became spear shafts.

flora-pigface.name: Pigface
flora-pigface.fact: A fleshy succulent that sprawls metres across the dunes and cliffs, with big purple-pink flowers around a white centre.
flora-pigface.noongar: people ate its fruit in late December, and used its juice to soothe burns, scalds and stings.

flora-rice-flower.name: Rice flower
flora-rice-flower.fact: Round heads of tiny tube flowers top every branch, usually pink, sometimes white. Gardeners grow it around the world. Ferruginea means “rust-coloured”.

flora-fan-flower.name: Fan-flower
flora-fan-flower.fact: Every flower looks cut in half, its petals all fanned out to one side. Scaevola means “left-handed” in Latin, and crassifolia “thick-leaved”.

flora-sea-spurge.name: Sea spurge
flora-sea-spurge.fact: An invader from southern Europe and North Africa, first recorded in WA at Albany in 1927. Its seeds float along the coast, and its bitter sap stings skin and eyes.

flora-spyridium.name: Basket bush
flora-spyridium.fact: Its name is Greek for “little basket”: each head of tiny cream flowers sits in a cup of white, furry leaves. Common on the dunes along this coast.

flora-cockies-tongues.name: Cockies’ tongues
flora-cockies-tongues.fact: Its bright red pea flowers light up the limestone cliffs in winter.
flora-cockies-tongues.noongar: people call the flower inji, and Injidup, one of the coast’s best-known surf breaks, takes its name from it.

sea-fauna-humpback.name: Humpback whale
sea-fauna-humpback.fact: They pass the Capes heading north to the Kimberley from June to August, and come back south from September to November. Mothers with tiny calves rest in Geographe Bay before the long swim to Antarctica.

sea-fauna-southern-right.name: Southern right whale
sea-fauna-southern-right.fact: Mothers bring their calves into the sheltered water of Flinders Bay at Augusta each winter. No dorsal fin, a V-shaped blow, and pale crusty patches on the head that tell one whale from another.

sea-fauna-dolphins.name: Bottlenose dolphins
sea-fauna-dolphins.fact: Families of dolphins play in the surf along the Capes, riding the same waves as the crew.
sea-fauna-dolphins.noongar: people call dolphins kwilena, and fished together with them.

sea-fauna-stingray.name: Smooth stingray
sea-fauna-stingray.fact: One of the biggest stingrays in the world: more than 2 metres across and up to 350 kilograms. At Hamelin Bay they glide right into the shallows.

sea-fauna-fur-seal.name: Long-nosed fur seal
sea-fauna-fur-seal.fact: Sealers wiped them out on the islands off Cape Leeuwin in the 1850s. In 1982, about 130 years later, they came back. They dive deeper than any other fur seal, past 300 metres.

sea-fauna-port-jackson.name: Port Jackson shark
sea-fauna-port-jackson.fact: A gentle reef shark that crunches sea urchins and shellfish with flat back teeth. It lays spiral, corkscrew-shaped egg cases that wedge into cracks in the reef.

sea-fauna-abalone.name: Roe’s abalone
sea-fauna-abalone.fact: Lives on the shallow limestone reefs right where the waves break, grazing on seaweed at night. Perth’s abalone season lasts just a few hours a year, and thousands crowd the reef for it.

sea-fauna-cuttlefish.name: Giant cuttlefish
sea-fauna-cuttlefish.fact: Changes colour in an instant, and raises its skin into bumps and frills to copy rock, sand or weed. It grows to about a metre long, yet lives only two to four years.

sea-fauna-leafy-seadragon.name: Leafy seadragon
sea-fauna-leafy-seadragon.fact: Most of WA’s sightings are along this coast, from Busselton to Augusta. Its leafy flaps make it look like drifting weed. The female lays her eggs under the male’s tail, and he carries them until they hatch.

sea-fauna-rock-lobster.name: Western rock lobster
sea-fauna-rock-lobster.fact: Its larvae drift 9 to 11 months far out in the Indian Ocean before swimming back to the reef. On the Capes, no lobster pots are allowed in the surfing zones.

sea-fauna-salmon.name: Australian salmon
sea-fauna-salmon.fact: Not a true salmon. They grow up in South Australia and Tasmania, then swim west to gather between Cape Leeuwin and Busselton in late autumn and early winter to spawn.
sea-fauna-salmon.noongar: people call the salmon ngari. Their yearly run matters so much to the Wadandi people that Ngari Capes Marine Park is named after it.

sea-fauna-herring.name: Australian herring
sea-fauna-herring.fact: Not a true herring. Its eggs and larvae drift south and east along the south coast, and the grown fish swim back west to spawn. A classic catch off the rocks and beaches.

sea-fauna-bronze-whaler.name: Bronze whaler
sea-fauna-bronze-whaler.fact: A slow-growing shark: it takes about 16 years to grow up, and a female can live past 30. It eats fish and squid, and even jellyfish.

sea-fauna-white-shark.name: White shark
sea-fauna-white-shark.fact: Warm-bodied: it can keep itself up to 14 °C warmer than the sea around it. At Margaret River’s Main Break, a receiver on the seabed hears tagged sharks and sends alerts to the SharkSmart WA app.

sea-fauna-tiger-shark.name: Tiger shark
sea-fauna-tiger-shark.fact: A tropical shark that visits cooler southern water now and then. Its stripes are boldest when it’s young, and often fade once it grows past about 3 metres.

sea-flora-kelp.name: Golden kelp
sea-flora-kelp.fact: The backbone of the Great Southern Reef, kelp forest that runs 8,000 km from Kalbarri round to Brisbane. Along the Capes, some kelp clones itself, its fronds growing new holdfasts that grip the reef.

sea-flora-posidonia.name: Seagrass
sea-flora-posidonia.fact: Not a seaweed but a flowering plant. Outside Shark Bay, Geographe Bay holds WA’s biggest seagrass meadows: nurseries for fish that also lock away carbon.

sea-flora-paddle-weed.name: Paddle weed
sea-flora-paddle-weed.fact: A tiny seagrass with oval leaves: a flowering plant, with separate male and female plants. Up north it’s a favourite food of dugongs, which is why it’s also called dugong grass.

sea-flora-asparagopsis.name: Harpoon weed
sea-flora-asparagopsis.fact: Barbed branches hook it onto other seaweeds. First described from Garden Island, WA, it holds a chemical that cuts the methane cattle burp when a pinch is added to their feed.

sea-flora-coralline.name: Coralline algae
sea-flora-coralline.fact: A seaweed that builds stone into its walls. The branching kinds bend at soft joints, like a string of beads. One kind grows on seagrass, and was collected at Canal Rocks near Yallingup.

sea-flora-sirophysalis.name: Three-node seaweed
sea-flora-sirophysalis.fact: Probably the first seaweed Europeans collected in Australia: William Dampier picked it up off the WA coast in 1699, and his specimen is still kept at Oxford.

sea-flora-laurencia.name: Laurencia
sea-flora-laurencia.fact: A red seaweed armed with bitter chemicals that put grazers off, though sea hares eat it anyway. In Hawaii one kind is used as a peppery seasoning.

sea-flora-sargassum.name: Sargassum
sea-flora-sargassum.fact: It floats on tiny gas-filled bladders, which reminded Portuguese sailors of grapes (sargaço). Lots of it washed up on the beach means a rough, swell-hit coast offshore.

sea-flora-sea-lettuce.name: Sea lettuce
sea-flora-sea-lettuce.fact: A bright green seaweed that thrives where the water is rich in nutrients, so it piles up near river mouths more than on the clean ocean coast. It’s edible, too.

sea-flora-strapweed.name: Western crayweed
sea-flora-strapweed.fact: One of the big habitat-making seaweeds of WA’s temperate coast, up to 2 metres long, on rough-water reefs like this one. The 2011 marine heatwave pushed its range back about 100 km.

birds-osprey.name: Osprey
birds-osprey.fact: A fish hawk that plunges feet-first into the sea. Ospreys nest on rock stacks along this coast and keep adding to the same nest year after year, until it can stand 2 metres tall.
birds-osprey.noongar: names for it include yoondoordo, and around Busselton it was recorded as koomagert.

birds-hooded-plover.name: Hooded plover
birds-hooded-plover.fact: Lays its eggs in a bare scrape in the sand above the tide line, on surf beaches like Gallows, South Point and Left Handers. Only about 14 pairs breed on the Capes, so give them room.

birds-oystercatcher.name: Sooty oystercatcher
birds-oystercatcher.fact: All black, with a red bill, eyes and legs. It works the rock platforms at low tide, and nests on lonely headlands like Gnarabup and Redgate. Females eat crabs, while males go for mussels and urchins.
birds-oystercatcher.noongar: names for it include kwikan. Around the Vasse it was recorded as kwee-kern.

birds-tropicbird.name: Red-tailed tropicbird
birds-tropicbird.fact: It dives for flying fish and squid far out at sea. Tropicbirds once nested on Sugarloaf Rock, off Cape Naturaliste, but they stopped around 2008. Now a pair or two nest on Rottnest instead.

birds-kestrel.name: Nankeen kestrel
birds-kestrel.fact: A small falcon that hangs in the wind on one spot, then drops onto grasshoppers, beetles and lizards. Nankeen is a yellowish cotton cloth, first made in Nanjing, China.

birds-sea-eagle.name: White-bellied sea eagle
birds-sea-eagle.fact: A big female can spread her wings 2.2 metres. Pairs stay together for life, and some nests are used for decades.
birds-sea-eagle.noongar: names for it include djilyon and ngoolar.

birds-albatross.name: Shy albatross
birds-albatross.fact: Australia’s own albatross: it breeds on only three islands off Tasmania, with wings up to 2.5 metres across. In winter, albatrosses glide past Cape Leeuwin and Cape Naturaliste.

birds-fairywren.name: Splendid fairywren
birds-fairywren.fact: The male turns electric blue for the breeding season, and courts females with pink and purple petals he plucks himself. In autumn the blue fades away.
birds-fairywren.noongar: names for it include djorrdjilya and djodjal.

birds-carnabys.name: Carnaby’s cockatoo
birds-carnabys.fact: Endangered, and found only in WA’s south-west. Flocks crack open banksia, hakea and marri for the seeds. Pairs mate for life, and one bird lived to 35.

birds-ringneck.name: Twenty-eight
birds-ringneck.fact: Named for its call, which sounds like “twenty-eight”. One early French listener heard “vingt-huit”.
birds-ringneck.noongar: names for it include dowarn, recorded around the Vasse, and doomolok.

birds-kookaburra.name: Laughing kookaburra
birds-kookaburra.fact: Not from here: it was brought over from the eastern states from 1883, hundreds of birds in all, probably for its name as a snake-killer. Family groups laugh together to mark their patch.

birds-brown-honeyeater.name: Brown honeyeater
birds-brown-honeyeater.fact: Only about 10 grams, but it has one of the loudest, sweetest songs of any Australian honeyeater.
birds-brown-honeyeater.noongar: names for it include djindjoko and kyeet.

birds-wattlebird.name: Red wattlebird
birds-wattlebird.fact: Australia’s second-biggest honeyeater, named for the pinkish-red wattles on its cheeks. It guards a flowering tree noisily against all comers.
birds-wattlebird.noongar: names for it include wodjalok. Around the Vasse it was recorded as dangong.

birds-spinebill.name: Western spinebill
birds-spinebill.fact: Found only in the south-west. Its long, curved bill reaches the nectar deep inside tube flowers, like kangaroo paw, that other honeyeaters can’t get to.

reptiles-bobtail.name: Bobtail
reptiles-bobtail.fact: Often found sunbaking right on the Cape to Cape Track. Its stumpy tail stores fat for the cold months, and a pair can meet up again every spring for 20 years.

reptiles-carpet-python.name: Carpet python
reptiles-carpet-python.fact: Not venomous, and mostly out at night, so lucky walkers rarely see one. A mother coils around her eggs and shivers her muscles to keep them warm until they hatch.

reptiles-marbled-gecko.name: Marbled gecko
reptiles-marbled-gecko.fact: Australia’s most southerly gecko. It drops its tail to get away from a predator, then spends about eight months growing a new one.

reptiles-bearded-dragon.name: Western bearded dragon
reptiles-bearded-dragon.fact: Waves a front leg to signal a rival or a mate, and the males bob their heads. Look for one basking on a fence post or a log.

reptiles-crowned-snake.name: Crowned snake
reptiles-crowned-snake.fact: A small snake of the south-west’s coastal heath, about 40 cm long, with a dark band across its neck like a crown. It hunts skinks and frogs. Mildly venomous: look, don’t touch.

reptiles-tiger-snake.name: Tiger snake
reptiles-tiger-snake.fact: Shy, and keeps clear of noisy people, but it will strike if cornered. On warm days snakes bask on the Cape to Cape Track: give them room, and they’ll slip away.

reptiles-dugite.name: Dugite
reptiles-dugite.fact: Found only in the south-west, in shades from grey to green to brown. Shy: leave it alone and it leaves you alone. If you meet one, stop, stay still and back away slowly.
reptiles-dugite.noongar: gave English its name: dugite comes from the Noongar word, recorded as dukitj and toogitj.

reptiles-heath-monitor.name: Heath monitor
reptiles-heath-monitor.fact: A goanna up to 1.5 metres long, black with fine yellow dots and pale bands right to the tip of its tail. A female can lay her eggs inside a termite mound, and the termites seal them in.

marsupials-ringtail-possum.name: Western ringtail possum
marsupials-ringtail-possum.fact: Critically endangered, and this coast is its stronghold. It lives on peppermint trees, curls its tail round the branches, and sleeps in a ball-shaped nest of shredded bark called a drey.

marsupials-quenda.name: Quenda
marsupials-quenda.fact: Often seen by day along the Cape to Cape Track. It digs up to 45 little pits a night hunting for food, turning over as much as four tonnes of soil a year.
marsupials-quenda.noongar: people call it kwenda, and English took its name from that. Around the Vasse it was recorded as gwinda.

marsupials-grey-kangaroo.name: Western grey kangaroo
marsupials-grey-kangaroo.fact: Plentiful in Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park. Big males can grow twice the size of females, and give off a curry-like smell that earns them the nickname “stinker”.
marsupials-grey-kangaroo.noongar: people call the male yongka, a name used right across the south-west.

marsupials-honey-possum.name: Honey possum
marsupials-honey-possum.fact: Lives on nothing but nectar and pollen, licked up with a bristle-tipped tongue. It has the smallest newborn young of any mammal, yet the longest sperm.
marsupials-honey-possum.noongar: people call it noolbenger, and for some Noongar families it is a totem animal.

marsupials-pygmy-possum.name: Western pygmy possum
marsupials-pygmy-possum.fact: Weighs as little as 8 grams. When food runs short it drops into torpor, cooling almost to the temperature of the air, and has been known to stay that way for 11 days.
marsupials-pygmy-possum.noongar: gave it its other name: mundarda comes from mandada.

marsupials-chuditch.name: Chuditch
marsupials-chuditch.fact: WA’s biggest meat-eating marsupial. It once lived across most of Australia, but now survives mainly in WA’s south-west, and the Leeuwin-Naturaliste Ridge is one of its refuges.
marsupials-chuditch.noongar: gave it its name. Around the Vasse it was recorded as ngooldjangit.

marsupials-tammar.kicker: Once lived here · Cape to Cape
marsupials-tammar.name: Tammar wallaby
marsupials-tammar.fact: Tammars once lived around Margaret River, but today they survive on islands and in inland reserves. A tammar was the first kangaroo Europeans ever saw, after the Batavia was wrecked in 1629.
marsupials-tammar.noongar: people around Margaret River and the Vasse called it bonin.
